newsitem.title: USA: Japan's Kato says appreciates US position on dlr.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Kato says appreciates US position on dlr.

text.p: Japan's Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs Takatoshi Kato said Wednesday that Japan appreciates remarks by U.S. authorities that a strong dollar is in the interest of the United States.

"We recognize U.S. authorities' reference to the effect that the strong dollar is in the interest of the United States. We appreciate those remarks by the U.S. authorities," Kato said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
Kato declined to comment on the level of the dollar, saying it was a common rule that the ministry stay away from making specific remarks about the dollar's level.
"We welcome the developments in recent periods. That's all I can say," Kato said when asked if a further strengthening of the dollar was in the interests of Japan.
Kato said it was difficult to say when Japanese interest rates would start rising again. "It depends certainly on the extent of Japan's economic recovery," he said.

Kator said the Ministry of Finance welcomed the recent comments by Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita that the primary objective of Japan's monetary policy for now was on making the economy more established.

Asked whether interest rates would stay low to the end of this year, Kato said he would not know about any specific time period. It was up to the Bank of Japan to decide monetary policy. "The BOJ, afterall, is an independent authority on monetary matters."
Asked whether further stimulus measures were required, Kato said the Ministry of Finance's current stance was to monitor economic developments.

Japan's economic recovery was becoming more firmly established in the view of Japan and the world. "If that is the case, the best thing is to watch how the economy develops and what kind of shape it would take," Kato said.

On private consumption, Kato said sales figures on durable goods like automobiles and electrical appliances were very good. "We're confident that private consumption is basically on a steady growth path," he said.
The rise in the unemployment rate was coming down little by little, Kato added.

"But the nature of the thing is such that any dramatic reduction of the unemployment rate may be difficult to expect," he said, pointing out that the unemployment figure was a lagging economic indicator.
